en: The Brief Method for the Study of the Vinaya by Bhikṣus of the Mūlasarvāstivāda School,
compiled by the Imperial Preceptor Bhikṣu Phags pa Blo gros rgyal mtshan (Phakpa Lhokdra Gyaltsen).
Homage to the Omniscient One!
The Vinaya Piṭaka, which teaches the training in higher ethical discipline (adhiśīla-śikṣā), consists of three parts:

first, the procedures for attaining the vows that have not yet been attained; second, the methods for guarding and maintaining the vows already attained so as not to transgress them; and third, the methods for restoration if a transgression has occurred. Regarding the first, the procedures for attaining the vows that have not yet been attained, there are four types.

It can act as an obstacle to attaining the vows; it can act as an obstacle to abiding in the vows; it can act as an obstacle to increasing virtuous qualities; and it can act as an obstacle to gracing the assembly. If none of these four adverse conditions are present, [the vow will be attained].
Furthermore, by means of the place of refuge, the physical form, the body, the recollection,
and the ritual procedure— if these five kinds of favorable conditions are fully present,
one then attains the restraint (*saṃvara*).
The meaning of these distinctions should be understood as it appears in the *Vinaya-kārikā*.
Second, regarding the five methods for upholding the restraint already obtained without transgression:
there are five kinds.

1. Guarding by relying on a preceptor (*ācārya*); 2. Guarding through the perception of the antidote (*pratipakṣasaṃjñā*); 3. Guarding by understanding the signs of what is to be abandoned; 4. Guarding by purifying one’s own ethical discipline (*śīla*); 5. Guarding by relying on the conditions for dwelling in happiness. Regarding the first, guarding by relying on a preceptor: if, after having received full ordination (*upasampadā*), ten years have been completed...
Among the twenty-one kinds of fivefold qualities (*pañcavarga-dharma*), fifteen qualities are required.
When a monk who understands the Vinaya seeks to become a preceptor (*upādhyāya*),
he must know what is to be done and what is not to be done.
One should inquire of that preceptor regarding all matters of practice;
acting in accordance with the instructions as the preceptor teaches,
one receives full ordination (*upasaṃpadā*) for oneself.
Once the three types of virtuous qualities have been perfected over a period of ten years or more,
one should rely upon that teacher.
Second, regarding guarding through the application of antidotes: at all times, one maintains mindfulness and clear comprehension without laxity.
By possessing these three factors, one eliminates all contrary phenomena.
One accomplishes all wholesome dharmas.

Third, regarding the comprehensive collection of those who understand the signs of what should be abandoned and what should be guarded and maintained, there are five sections totaling two hundred and fifty-three rules.
Within these dharmas that should be abandoned, one possesses pure precepts.
Or, one may possess the precepts that ought to be repaired;
possessing mindfulness and awareness,
and provided it was not due to an initial lapse, one does not abandon the training rules.
Regarding the first *pārājika* offense among the training rules (*śikṣāpada*) that are not to be transgressed:
it concerns a bhikṣu within the three paths.
If one practices impure conduct along any one of these paths,
one commits the first *pārājika* offense.
If one steals the property of another that does not belong to oneself, [one likewise commits a *pārājika* offense].
One commits the second *pārājika* offense.
One commits the third *pārājika* offense by taking the life of another person or a human fetus, excluding one's own body.
One who falsely claims to have attained the superhuman states (uttarimanussadhamma) commits the fourth pārājika offense.
These are the four pārājika offenses.
These all sever the very root of right precepts.
The first section is concluded.
Regarding the twenty-third section, the Saṃghāvaśeṣa:
If one intentionally emits semen;
if one, with a defiled mind, touches the body of a woman;
or if one speaks with a woman using coarse and evil names concerning sexual desire.
If one praises oneself before a woman,
saying that one may provide the service of sexual desire as an offering,
or acts as a husband to her; this constitutes [an offense].
If one requests land and building materials from others to construct a dwelling on a site that is unsuitable,
and it is indeed an unsuitable site.
Regarding those who establish monasteries:
if one slanders a bhikṣu with groundless accusations of having committed a pārājika offense,
or if one does so groundlessly on account of some minor cause;
Those who slanderfully claim that a bhikṣu has committed a pārājika offense;
those who cause a schism in the Saṃgha;
or those who assist in causing a schism in the Saṃgha.
If one has defiled a household and thereby caused the Saṃgha to expel him,
or if he has slandered the Saṃgha, then when other bhikṣus,
out of compassion for his own discipline, wish to exhort him;
Regarding the discourse on the various Saṃghas: "Because of all my rules of training, do not speak against me;
those who reject them shall be in violation."
These thirteen dharmas must be repaired by the Saṃgha;
therefore, they are called *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
The second section is concluded.
The third section on *pāyattika* offenses consists of two parts.

First, regarding the thirty *naiḥsargika-pāyattikas*, the first ten of this initial group concern the improper storage of robes beyond ten nights without having performed the ritual consecration (*adhiṣṭhāna*).
If one has consecrated the three robes and stays apart from them for more than one night,
and if the three robes are insufficient and one must rely on others, [one may remain separated].
If one has kept such items for more than thirty nights;
or if one causes a nun who is not a relative to wash or dye one's robes;
or if one receives robes from a bhikṣuṇī.
If one possesses the three robes but begs for clothing from a householder,
or if one does not possess the three robes oneself and begs from another,
yet begs in excess of what is required.
If another person wishes to give an object but has not yet given it, and one asks for it;
or if various other persons each wish to give an object but have not yet given it, and one asks for them.
If the items have already been sent and are unfit to be made into robes,
yet one requests them more than three times verbally,
or seeks them more than three times by remaining silent; [one incurs an offense].
The first cycle of ten items is finished.
Regarding the second cycle of ten items: if one makes a new bedding from silk-cotton, or if one makes a new bedding from pure black wool.
If one makes a bedding mat by mixing black and white wool;
or if one makes a second bedding mat before six years have passed;
or if one makes a new sitting mat without using an old one.
The length and width shall be one span of the Buddha’s hand;
it is for use as an upper layer spread over new [mats].
If there is no person available to carry the wool, [one may keep it oneself].
If one carries wool oneself over a distance of three yojanas,
or if a person carrying it themselves carries it for a distance of one li, [it constitutes an offense].
If one causes a non-relative bhikṣuṇī to card wool;
if one keeps precious gems for oneself, touches them personally, or instructs others to touch them;
or if one engages in the lending and borrowing of wealth to seek profit.
Regarding buying and selling:
the second set of ten items is finished.
As for the third set of ten items, if one possesses a standard measuring vessel that has not been consecrated and keeps it for more than ten nights, [it constitutes an offense].
If one already possesses a bowl yet seeks another,
or if one causes a non-relative weaver to weave a garment without providing wages for its completion; these constitute offenses.
If another person has someone else weave a robe for one's own sake,
and for the benefit of oneself instructs the weaver to increase its size,
yet after having given the robe or bowl to a bhikṣu, subsequently takes it back; [this constitutes an offense].
If gains are obtained during the summer retreat (varṣā), they are to be taken within the retreat;
or they may be distributed during the retreat;
or after the retreat has concluded and the invitation ceremony (pravāraṇā) has been performed.
Regarding those who do not share their gains:
if a bhikṣu dwelling in an araṇya leaves his Dharma robes within a village or hamlet for more than six nights.
If one does not later go to the place where the robe was left,
or if it was from a forest hermitage (āraṇya),
or if it was a rain-bathing robe requested one month before the retreat (varṣā).
Or, having kept [an item] for more than half a month after the end of the rainy season retreat,
one may wish to give it to the community of monks or to a single monk.
Regarding those who have diverted [the goods] into their own possession:
if they are capable of accepting or rejecting the four kinds of medicine,
yet each keeps them beyond the limit.
This concludes the third cycle of the ten types of thirty *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* rules.
Regarding the first cycle of the ten types of *pāyattika* rules within the second set of nine cycles:
If a bhikṣu intentionally speaks falsehoods;
if he speaks of the faults of other bhikṣus;
or if he uses double-tongued speech to cause a rift between two bhikṣus or others.
If, after a dispute among bhikṣus has been settled through reconciliation,
one should again raise that dispute;
or if one should preach the Dharma to a laywoman when no man is present.
If one recites or instructs the Dharma in unison with a person who has not yet received full ordination;
or if one knows that another bhikṣu has committed an offense involving defeat (pārājika) or an offense requiring suspension (saṃghāvaśeṣa).
Regarding each instance of speaking to a layperson:

if one truthfully claims to have attained a state of superior human dharma (*uttara-manuṣya-dharma*) before someone who has not yet received full ordination (*upasampadā*) and who has not yet realized the Noble Truths (*ārya-satya*).
If one slanders a monk who serves the Saṃgha and is without fault,
saying that he gives property belonging to the Saṃgha or personal items to his acquaintances;
or if, on the day of the Poṣadha, while the minor precepts are being recited...
They spoke with contempt, saying:
"Why is it necessary to preach such trivial precepts?
Let other bhikṣus hear them!"
The first cycle of ten types is finished.
Regarding the second cycle of ten types: if one destroys seeds or cuts green grass and trees;
or if one feels resentment toward, disparages, or treats with contempt a monk who serves as an official of the Saṃgha.
If one violates or causes distress to a fellow practitioner of the Dharma who speaks words of benefit and instruction;
or if, with a negligent mind, one places the bedding and requisites of the Saṃgha in the open air.
If one spreads grass or leaves within a monastic dwelling and does not remove or sweep them after use,
and if the monks are then expelled from the monastery, [the fault belongs to that person].
If, at a monastery where the Saṃgha resides, later-arriving bhikṣus bully those who have resided there first;
or if the monastery buildings are not secure and one sits or lies upon an upper story or a loft using a bed with removable legs.
If one uses water containing insects for the sake of others,
or when constructing the walls of a monastery or saṃghārāma,
except for the permitted amount.
Regarding the excessive piling up:
the second round of ten items is finished.
As for the ten items of the third round, if the Saṃgha has not yet appointed [an official], [the procedure continues as follows].
Regarding one who intentionally goes to instruct a bhikṣuṇī:
if one instructs a bhikṣuṇī until sunset;
or if, while lacking such an intention, one speaks disparagingly of another.
Regarding these minor instructions on food and drink for bhikṣuṇīs:
if a bhikṣu gives clothing to a bhikṣuṇī,
or if a bhikṣu sews clothing for a bhikṣuṇī.
If a bhikṣu travels on a road as a companion to a bhikṣuṇī;
or if a bhikṣu boards a boat together with a bhikṣuṇī;
or if a bhikṣu sits in a secluded place together with a woman.
If a bhikṣu stands in a secluded place with a woman; or if,
because of a bhikṣuṇī’s praise, he accepts food from a layperson—
this concludes the third set of ten [offenses].
Regarding the ten types [of offenses] for the fourth time: if one eats a second meal while there is no gain of requisites during a single meal;
or if one stays overnight at the residence of non-Buddhists and accepts a second meal, and so forth.
If a bhikṣu has finished eating his fill and eats again without performing the *kṛta-śeṣa* rite,
or if a bhikṣu who is begging for alms [accepts food] from a householder...
Regarding "one who has received two or three bowls of food":
if a bhikṣu, having already finished eating his fill, is urged by another to eat more;
or if a bhikṣu is apart from the regular place where the Saṃgha eats.
Each has no food of their own;
as for those who eat separately with three bhikṣus or others,
if they eat from the time the sun sets until the appearance of the dawn light.
Regarding eating at an improper time:
if a bhikṣu eats, whether for himself or on behalf of another,
food that he has stored up.
If one eats food that was not offered or received,
or if one requests choice foods from a donor,
this concludes the ten items of the fourth section.
Regarding the ten types for the fifth time: if one uses water containing insects or similar for one's own personal use;
or if, when a householder is engaged in unchaste conduct, one sits in the same room as him.
If one engages in impure conduct while at home;
or if one stands listening while others are in the same room;
or if one gives food to naked ascetics (nirgrantha).
If one observes those who are preparing their armies for battle,
or if, without a valid reason, one stays for more than two nights within a military encampment,
or if one disrupts the established military formations.
If one strikes a bhikṣu;
or if one raises a hand toward a bhikṣu;
or if one knowingly conceals a grave offense committed by another bhikṣu.
The ten items for the fifth round are finished.

Regarding the ten items for the sixth round: if a donor, seeking to settle a grievance, intends to give food to a bhikṣu but obstructs him so as not to let him receive it, causing him to fast on that very day.
If one touches fire, or if,
while a *bhikṣu* is performing a formal ritual (*karmavācanā*),
one has given their consent (*chanda*) and subsequently regrets it; [in these cases, there is an offense].
If a bhikṣu stays for more than one night within a distance of one fathom from a person who has not yet received full ordination, [he commits an offense].
If one claims that sexual desire does not constitute an obstacle, or holds to wrong views regarding administrative duties;
or if, when the Saṃgha offers admonition, one does not relinquish such views;
or if one associates with a monk dispatched by the Saṃgha as a companion.
If one knows that a śrāmaṇera has been expelled,
yet accepts him as a follower, treats him with benefit, and dwells together with him;
or if one makes use of his uncolored robes, white lay garments, bedding, and so forth.
If one touches, or instructs another to touch, treasures belonging to others or other precious and excellent objects,
starting from the first day of the fourth month.
Until the fifteenth day of the sixth month;
excluding these two and a half months,
during all other times.
If one bathes before the half-month has passed, the tenth item of the sixth cycle is concluded.
Regarding the ten items of the seventh cycle:
if one intentionally takes the life of a living being, [it is a transgression].
If one says to a bhikṣu, "You are not a bhikṣu," causing him momentary displeasure;
or if one strikes or pokes a bhikṣu with a finger.

If one plays in the water, or if one stays alone with a laywoman in the same room until dawn; or if one stays alone with a female ascetic in the same room until dawn; or if one stays alone with a woman who has not yet reached puberty in the same room until dawn; or if one stays alone with a eunuch in the same room until dawn; or if one stays alone with a male novice in the same room until dawn—these are offenses of expiation involving forfeiture. If a bhikṣu, out of fear, causes another bhikṣu to conceal his robe,
or if he gives a bhikṣu a robe and does not return it when it is taken back, [he commits an offense].
If a bhikṣu, without basis or with only a minor cause,
slanders another by falsely claiming they have committed a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense;
or if he travels together with a laywoman on the same path without any other man present.
The ten items for the seventh round are finished.
As for the ten items for the eighth round: if one travels on the same road as merchants who are traveling together with thieves or evading taxes;
or if one knows that [the candidate] is not yet twenty years of age.
Regarding those who confer full ordination (*upasampadā*):
if one digs even a single handful of earth from solid ground,
or if one accepts an invitation from a layperson.
Having resided for more than four months,
if one does not abide by the regulations of the Saṃgha but instead slanders them,
they address the bhikṣus as follows:
"You who are foolish and ignorant,
if there are bhikṣus engaged in a dispute whom you wish to have go elsewhere to hear their discourse,
[you may do so] from the place where the saṃgha is performing its formal ritual (karmavācanā)."
Without asking a single bhikṣu, he rose from his seat and went far away to a place beyond the range of hearing,
such as a place where the Saṃgha should be venerated with faith, or the offices of the Saṃgha’s attendants.
Those who lack reverence and faith, who do not comply with the teachings,
who drink various intoxicants such as liquor,
or who do not inquire of the bhikṣus and others.
Regarding those who enter a village toward evening:
this concludes the ten items of the eighth round.
As for the ten items of the ninth round: if a bhikṣu has accepted an invitation to a meal at a lay household.
Before noon, one should go to visit the remaining three households and so forth; or else,
toward evening, with the exception of places where the Saṃgha assembles.
Regarding "entering the other four types of households" and so forth:
it refers to the time after sunset,
when the crimson glow has already vanished.
Before the first light of dawn has appeared,
he enters the palace of the consecrated king,
or the inner quarters of the queen and consorts.
If, on the day of the Poṣadha, while the Prātimokṣa Sūtra is being recited,
one says regarding the minor precepts:
"I have only now come to know such minor precepts."
These are matters that one ought to train in,
yet which some treat with contempt and derision: namely, using ivory and the like for needle cases,
or sitting or lying on beds whose legs exceed the prescribed measure.
If one uses a monastic bedding or mat that has been stained with cotton wool or similar substances to make a sitting cloth (niṣīdana), [it is not permissible].
It should be three cubits in length and two cubits plus six finger-breadths in width.
If one makes it exceeding these measurements,
it is [only] for the purpose of making a wound-covering cloth.
It should be six cubits in length and three cubits in width.
If one makes a rain-bath robe exceeding these measurements,
it should be nine cubits in length and three cubits and eighteen finger-widths in width.
If one makes a robe exceeding this measure,
or if one instructs another to make it, such that it is made according to the measure of a Buddha’s robe; or...
One commits a *pāyattika* offense.
Regarding the measurement of the Tathāgata’s robe:
its length is that of a medium-sized person.
A person is fifteen cubits in height and nine cubits in width; this is it.
The ninth cycle of ten items is completed.
Altogether, the ninety *pāyattika* rules are finished.
The fourth set of four *pāyantikās*: if, whether in a village or outside a village,
on a road or near a road, one receives food from a bhikṣuṇī.
If there is a bhikṣuṇī within the house of a layperson who,
having been assigned her turn, does not stop eating when instructed,
and if this is a household restricted by the Saṃgha;
"Taking food in return" refers to when one has been assigned to guard against dangers on a journey,
yet fails to provide such guard.
The four *pāṭidesanīyas* concerning eating while seated are concluded.
Fifth, among the one hundred and twelve rules that should be studied: one should wear the *antarvāsaka* neatly and properly adjusted.
It should not be too high nor too low;
the corners of the robe should not resemble an elephant's trunk,
nor should they be like a *tāla* leaf.
The robe should not be gathered into a ball;
it should not have a snake-head fold; it should be worn evenly and neatly;
it should be neither too high nor too low.
When walking for alms, one should well-guard the conduct of body and speech;
wear the Dharma robes neatly;
walk without making noise and look about without distraction.
When walking, one should walk while observing a distance of one fathom.
If entering a village, one must not walk with the head covered by the robe,
nor should one walk with the robe tucked up.
One must not walk with one's shoulder against the hem of the robe.
One must not walk with both hands crossed behind the neck.
One must not walk with both hands clasped behind the head;
one must not walk by jumping;
one must not walk by kicking out the feet.
One must not walk squatting;
one must not walk on one's toes;
one must not walk with hands placed upon the hips.
One must not walk while swaying the body;
one must not walk while swinging the arms;
one must not walk while shaking the head.
One must not walk with shoulders rubbing together.
One must not walk holding hands.
Unless invited, one must not sit upon bedding or mats in the home of a layperson.
One should not sit without careful observation.
One must not sit down heavily, casting the body forward.
One must not sit with the feet crossed.
One must not sit with the legs crossed.
One must not sit with the inner and outer ankles pressed together.
When sitting upon a bed, [one should likewise observe these rules].
One must not tuck one's legs under when entering beneath a bed;
one must not sit with legs crossed or sit with legs spread wide.
One should receive food with a focused and upright mind.
One must not receive food until the bowl is full.
One must not receive vegetables and other foods in equal portions.
One should receive food according to the order of the seating.
One should look toward the bowl when receiving food.
When the food has not yet arrived, one must not extend the bowl in advance in anticipation of receiving more.
One must not cover vegetables with solid food.
One must not cover food with vegetables.
When receiving food, one must not place the bowl atop the food; rather, one should eat with focused attention.
One must not form morsels that are excessively small.
One must not form an excessively large morsel when eating;

If the food has not yet reached the mouth, one must not open the mouth to wait for it.
One must not speak with food in the mouth.
One must not eat with knitted brows.
One must not make smacking sounds while eating.
One must not eat by blowing air upon the food;
one must not eat by puffing air upon it;
one must not eat by extending the tongue.
One must not eat by picking up individual grains.
When receiving food, one must not scold or laugh at others.

One must not make clicking sounds with the tongue while eating.
One must not bite off half a morsel of food.
One must not lick the hands.
One must not shake one's hands.
One must not scrape the bowl or lick it with the tongue.
One must not shake out the food from the bowl or pile the food into the shape of a stūpa while eating.
One should not eat by damaging the food.
One must not laugh at the bowl of a fellow bhikṣu sitting beside one.
One must not hold the water-pitcher with soiled hands.
One must not sprinkle rice-water upon a bhikṣu sitting nearby.

One should discard leftover food;
it must not be placed back inside the bowl.
If there is no mat upon the ground, one should not place the bowl on the edge of a stream.
One must not place the bowl in a precarious location.
One must not place the bowl on a steep cliff.
One must not place the bowl [in such places].
One must not stand while washing the bowl by a stream;
one must not wash the bowl in a precarious place;
one must not wash the bowl on a steep cliff.
One must not wash the bowl while facing a torrential current;
one must not use the bowl to scoop up water.

If another person is seated on a high seat and oneself is seated on a low seat,

If another person is walking in front and oneself is walking behind, [one should not preach the Dharma].
One should not preach the Dharma to them.
If the person is walking on the path while one is walking off the path,
one should not preach the Dharma to them.
One should not preach the Dharma to a person whose head is covered;
one should not preach the Dharma to a person who has tucked up their robe;
one should not preach the Dharma to a person who is gathering up their robe or patting their shoulder.
One should not preach the Dharma to someone who has both hands crossed behind the neck;
one should not preach the Dharma to someone who has both hands crossed behind the head;
one should not preach the Dharma to someone who has fashioned their hair into a topknot.
One should not preach the Dharma to those wearing hats;
one should not preach the Dharma to those wearing crowns;
one should not preach the Dharma to those wearing flower garlands.
One should not preach the Dharma to someone with their head wrapped in a turban.
One should not preach the Dharma to someone riding an elephant.
One should not preach the Dharma to someone riding a horse.
One should not preach the Dharma to those traveling in a carriage.
One should not preach the Dharma to those seated upon various objects.
One should not preach the Dharma to those wearing boots.
One should not preach the Dharma to those carrying staves, nor to those carrying swords,
nor to those carrying parasols.
One should not preach the Dharma to those who carry swords;
one should not preach the Dharma to those who carry weapons;
one should not preach the Dharma to those who wear armor.
One must not stand while defecating or urinating.
One must not defecate, urinate, spit, sneeze, or vomit in water.
One must not defecate, urinate, snot, spit, or vomit upon green grass.
